newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ASM LITHO SAYS DEMAND GROWING.
newsitem.headline: ASM LITHO SAYS DEMAND GROWING.

text.p: Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASM Lithography NV, announcing a big rise in first half 1997 net profit, said on Wednesday that demand for its products was increasing in the second half.

ASML said earlier net income in the first six months of 1997 rose to 147 million guilders from 100.7 million, including a 31.1 million extraordinary gain from the sale of a small share stake in one of its main suppliers.
"We're seeing demand picking up. We expect 1997 to show clear growth compared to 1996," ASML chief executive Willem Maris told journalists at a results presentation.
Maris said the semiconductor equipment market always lagged behind the actual semiconductor market, which declined in March 1996 and started to recover at the beginning of this year.

"The equipment market started to decline in the second half of 1996. The first half of this year was pretty lean but we came through it very well because we were able to deliver new technology," Maris said.

He said figures from industry analysts pointed to world semiconductor sales of $318 billion in 2001, compared to $142 billion in 1996. Semiconductor equipment sales are seen bouncing to $40.1 billion in 2001 from $21.7 billion in 1996.
"We now see the semiconductor market is becoming more aggressive, especially in memory chips," he added.

Maris said ASML was continuing to gain market share against its main rivals, advancing towards its strategic aim of overhauling number two equipment maker Canon and gaining ground on market leader Nikon .

"I don't know exactly how much we're gaining on Canon. We are gaining on them. The reason is that we have new customers coming in and we're not losing any. We've taken customers in the past from Canon and Nikon," he said.

Maris said industry figures showed Nikon had 47 percent of the market during 1996, Canon had 24.1 percent and ASML 20.2 percent. Earlier this year industry estimates put Nikon on 45 percent for 1996, Canon on 26 percent and ASML on 19 percent.

Gross margins at ASML dipped in the first half to 40 percent from 41.8 percent because the company had been selling new generation "deep UV" machines which had a lower margin than its older "I-line" machines.
Maris said the company had a strategic target for gross margins of 45 percent but declined to say when that might be reached.

"We think that 45 percent when you look to the equipment industry is a very reasonable gross margin. It is higher, by the way, than what Nikon is doing," Maris told Reuters immediately after the news conference.

"If when we can develop faster and better than the competition and have a more significant difference in the productivity of these machines, then we can increase the price and the opposition can't," he said.
